responses_archetypeVariants.defender: The committed interlocutor upgrades the charge from an insult into an epistemology: not "you're spoiled" but "your comfort disqualifies your testimony — you have never lived the suffering you presume to legislate about, so your standpoint is illegitimate and the argument doesn't reach." Concede the real core, because there is one and denying it forfeits the exchange: lived deprivation can grant access to facts the comfortable genuinely miss, and standpoint epistemology is not a fraud. Then refuse the move it is actually making. Standpoint can make you a better witness to a premise; it cannot convert a valid argument into an invalid one. The asymmetry of suffering and the consent objection do not check the arguer's passport or bank balance — they are evaluated by the same standard whether voiced from a township or a penthouse, and "you haven't suffered enough to say this" is the genetic fallacy wearing the robes of epistemic humility. Two things finish it. First, the weapon turns in the hand: if only the sufferer may speak to suffering, the comfortable natalist defending procreation is disqualified first and worst — he is legislating the entire welfare of a being whose guaranteed suffering he will not personally carry, from exactly the position of comfort he just ruled out of order. Run consistently, the standpoint objection silences the procreator before it ever reaches the antinatalist. Second, and quieter: by invoking the developing world's agony as the "real" suffering against which first-world pessimism looks frivolous, the objector has conceded the major premise outright. The suffering is real, severe, and unconsented-to — which is the antinatalist's claim, now granted in the course of attacking it. The dodge runs only by handing over exactly what it set out to deny.
